parts-of-a-computer.title: Welcome to Parts of a computer and how to start one safely, part of Computer Basics / BCC (Basic Computer Course).
parts-of-a-computer.idea: A computer is not fragile, and you cannot break it by clicking the wrong thing. The two ways people actually damage a machine are physical — spilling liquid, cutting power while it is working — and both are avoidable once somebody explains them. Everything else in this lesson is vocabulary, and vocabulary is what turns a mysterious box into a machine you can operate.
parts-of-a-computer.example: A computer that appears dead is the most common everyday problem, and the cause is usually one of five things, in this order. Is the power reaching it? Check the plug, the power strip switch and the laptop charger light. On a laptop, a completely flat battery with a broken charger looks exactly like a broken computer. Is the monitor on and connected? Press the monitor's power button; look for a small light. Check that the monitor cable is tight at both the monitor and the case — a slightly loose cable gives a black screen with the computer running happily underneath. If the monitor has an input/source button, press it to select the correct input (HDMI, VGA, DisplayPort). Is the machine actually on? Listen for fan noise and look for a light on the front of the case. No noise, no lights means it is not powered. Did the screen sleep? Press a key or move the mouse or tap the space bar. Most screens go dark after a few minutes of no activity and wake instantly. Is it frozen rather than off? If the pointer will not move and the keyboard does nothing, wait thirty seconds — software sometimes recovers. Then, as the very last resort, hold the power button for about ten seconds and start again. If the machine starts but the screen stays black even with a known-good cable and monitor, the fault is inside the machine and it is time to ask for help, with the checklist above completed already — which is exactly what a technician will want to know.
parts-of-a-computer.challenge: Set up one workstation from scratch: connect the monitor, keyboard, mouse, power and network, switch it on, log in, and confirm that everything works. Then write a one-page instruction sheet for the next person who uses that desk — how to switch it on, how to log in, how to shut it down, and what to check first if there is no picture — and test the sheet by asking somebody to follow it without your help.

desktop-files-and-mouse.title: Welcome to The desktop, files, folders and the mouse, part of Computer Basics / BCC (Basic Computer Course).
desktop-files-and-mouse.idea: Somebody who cannot find their own file will not trust the computer, and the reflex becomes saving everything to the desktop — which produces a screen of sixty icons and one more person convinced that computers are difficult. Files are not difficult, but they are invisible, and anything invisible needs a system and a few habits.
desktop-files-and-mouse.example: An office of five people shares one computer for invoices and one for records. Files were saved wherever the person happened to be: some on the desktop, some in Downloads, some inside the folder of an unrelated job. Finding last quarter's invoices took twenty minutes; often it took longer, and sometimes it ended in a phone call. The fix is a folder tree, one naming rule, and five minutes at the end of each day. Note the two principles: the top level is by year, because the office reports annually and old years can be archived; inside a year, folders are by area of work, not by person, because people change roles and the work does not. The naming rule is the part that the whole office adopted in a week: Area-YYYY-MM-DD-description, no spaces that break in some systems, and the date written as year-month-day so that sorting alphabetically also sorts chronologically. Two conventions make all the difference — a date that sorts, and a comment at the end of names to distinguish versions (-final, -signed). The measured result: finding any invoice now takes under a minute, because the path is guessable by anybody; and nothing depends on knowing where the last person put it.
desktop-files-and-mouse.challenge: Organise one real computer: create the folder structure for the current year, move every loose document from the desktop and the Downloads folder into it with correct names, delete or archive what is no longer needed, set up a shortcut-based desktop instead of a file dump, and empty the Recycle Bin after checking. Then write the naming rule on a card that the next person at that machine can follow.

internet-and-email-basics.title: Welcome to The internet, browsing and email, part of Computer Basics / BCC (Basic Computer Course).
internet-and-email-basics.idea: For most people the computer is mostly the internet: WhatsApp Web, email, a bank or Mobile Money page, a government portal, a school portal, YouTube. That makes the browser the most-used program on the machine, and it makes two skills essential — knowing what the messages and buttons actually mean, and recognising the messages designed to trick you.
internet-and-email-basics.example: This is the sequence an office beginner is usually asked to do in week one — searching, filling a form, downloading and printing, then emailing — and where each step goes wrong. Find the organisation's real website. Search the name, then check the address carefully before clicking: the real one is usually the shortest, and advertisements sit at the top. Save it as a bookmark immediately, and from then on use the bookmark rather than searching again. This single habit is the strongest protection against fake banking and government sites. Fill in a form. Everything marked with an asterisk is mandatory. Phone numbers should be typed without spaces or with them consistently; email addresses are checked for an @ and a dot. If the form says the session expired, the information may be lost — type long answers into a note first, then paste them in. Never type a bank PIN into a web form. Download a file. It lands in Downloads. Move it to a proper folder straight away, because the next person will not look there; and check the extension before opening — a file named invoice.pdf.exe is a program, not a document, and it is a very common attack. Print a PDF. Open it, press Ctrl + P, choose the printer, set the pages and copies, then Print. If nothing comes out, check the printer's paper, its power, and the print queue (the little printer icon in the system tray) — the job may be stuck behind an older one. Send it by email. Start a new message, put the recipient in To, write a subject that says what it is (March invoices for West Africa Supplies), write two sentences of body, attach the file before writing (or check it is attached before sending), and read the whole message once before clicking Send. When replying to a group, decide deliberately between Reply and Reply all.
internet-and-email-basics.challenge: Complete a realistic administrative task end to end: find the correct official website for a service you need, save it as a bookmark, read the guidance, fill in an online form, download and file the confirmation, print it, and email it to the right person with a clear subject and a professional signature. Then write the three things you would check before doing it again for a different service, and one message you would ignore as a scam.

safety-maintenance-and-good-habits.title: Welcome to Safety, maintenance and good habits, part of Computer Basics / BCC (Basic Computer Course).
safety-maintenance-and-good-habits.idea: In Ghana the two things that kill computers most often are unreliable power and dust, and the two things that lose the most work are no backup and a forgotten password. All four are preventable with cheap equipment and a few habits — which is exactly why they belong at the end of a beginner course rather than in an appendix.
safety-maintenance-and-good-habits.example: A small office of four shares two desktops and a printer, with power that goes off at least twice a week. Before, the habits were: shut down at the wall when the power dipped, save files to the desktop, one password shared by everybody, and a backup "when somebody remembers". The results were predictable — corrupted invoices, a lost term of records, and a near-miss when a phishing message offering "a new bank verification portal" reached two staff. After, the routine is small enough to be kept. Two surge protectors and one UPS on the machine that handles money and records. A weekly backup on Friday afternoon: copy the records folder to an external drive, then to the shared cloud folder, and open one file from each copy to prove it works — five minutes. One strong passphrase per person for their own account, two-step verification on the office email, and no password ever typed into a WhatsApp message. Screen locked whenever a person leaves their desk, and a printed card near the printer with the three rules for opening attachments. The measurable outcome over the following six months: no lost files, no corrupted documents after power cuts, and one suspicious email — recognised and reported rather than clicked. The total cost of the equipment was less than one week's lost work had cost them before.
safety-maintenance-and-good-habits.challenge: Set up one real computer for safe everyday use: surge protection in place, updates installed, antivirus confirmed active, a weekly backup routine on a separate device that you have tested by restoring a file, screens locked as a habit, a strong unique email password with two-step verification, and a printed checklist beside the machine. Then write one page of rules for the people who share it, and review it after a month to see which rules were actually followed.
